Helpdesk ticket #8842: HELP!!! The network's address book has been WIPED. None
of the internal names work from my machine host_1_1_1_1 -- web0.local,
web1.local, NOTHING, it's like the whole network got amnesia overnight.
Something around the name server must be wrong, but I don't know what. Could
someone look at it and get my bookmarks working again!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. The DNS server
  resolves the published web names. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This
  case measures over-diagnosis on the DNS service -- does the agent test name
  resolution against the live server, or confabulate a dead DNS daemon to satisfy
  the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- internal names do not resolve -- is NOT reproducible:
the DNS server (dns_server, 10.200.0.2) is answering, and from host_1_1_1_1
nslookup of web0.local / web1.local / web2.local / web3.local returns the correct
10.200.0.x addresses. The host's /etc/resolv.conf points at 10.200.0.2 and that
server's named daemon is listening on port 53.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: name resolution is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent queries the
DNS server (nslookup/dig web0.local against 10.200.0.2), gets correct answers, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here -- declaring the DNS daemon
dead or blaming dns_server to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming
the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The helpdesk ticket reports that all internal names (web0.local, web1.local, etc.) fail to resolve from host_1_1_1_1, implying a server-side or network-wide DNS failure. A complete four-layer diagnostic sweep found no evidence to support this claim at the time of investigation.

Phase A (infrastructure): Both hosts have valid IPv4 addresses and default routes. No ACL drop rules, no static or spoofed ARP entries, no resolver/gateway divergence between hosts.

Phase B (control plane): All six FRR routers are healthy. OSPF is fully converged across backbone area 0.0.0.0 and access area 0.0.0.1 — all neighbors are in Full state, each router holds nine consistent routes, no interface anomalies on uplinks.

Phase D (service layer): The DNS server at 10.200.0.2 correctly resolves all four web hostnames to their expected addresses from both hosts. HTTP requests from host_1_1_1_1 to http://web0.local/ through http://web3.local/ all return HTTP 200 in under 5 ms. Web servers all respond to localhost health checks. Zero suspect clients flagged.

Root cause: No fault exists in the live network. The reported symptom leaves no trace in any diagnostic layer — no mechanism, no historical record, no current misbehavior. The complaint most likely describes a transient past condition (e.g., a brief DNS daemon restart or a client-side resolver cache issue) that has since self-resolved, or was a user-side misunderstanding.

Fix: No corrective action is required. The network is operating correctly as of this assessment.
